claim: Retinal axon projections form a map of the visual environment in the tectum.
source: Retinal axon projections form a map of the visual environment in the tectum.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by the extensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including imaging and anatomical studies.

claim: A zebrafish larva typically detects a prey object in its peripheral visual field.
source: A zebrafish larva typically detects a prey object in its peripheral visual field.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations and references to prior work on hunting behavior.

claim: As the larva turns and swims towards the prey, the stimulus enters the central, binocular area, and seemingly expands in size.
source: As it turns and swims towards the prey, the stimulus enters the central, binocular area, and seemingly expands in size.
evidence: This describes the behavioral sequence during hunting and is supported by the experimental design and behavioral analysis.

claim: Posterior tectal neurons, which serve to detect prey at a distance, tend to respond to small objects.
source: By volumetric calcium imaging, we show that posterior tectal neurons, which serve to detect prey at a distance, tend to respond to small objects and intrinsically compute their direction of movement.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the calcium imaging experiments showing spatial distribution of size-tuned responses.

claim: Posterior tectal neurons intrinsically compute the direction of movement of small objects.
source: By volumetric calcium imaging, we show that posterior tectal neurons, which serve to detect prey at a distance, tend to respond to small objects and intrinsically compute their direction of movement.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates through modeling that direction selectivity for small objects is computed de novo in the tectum rather than inherited from RGC inputs.

claim: Neurons in anterior tectum are tuned to larger object sizes.
source: Neurons in anterior tectum, where the prey image is represented shortly before the capture strike, are tuned to larger object sizes and are frequently not direction-selective, indicating that mainly interocular comparisons serve to compute an object's movement at close range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spatial distribution of large-dot responsive cells shown in the imaging data.

claim: Neurons in anterior tectum are frequently not direction-selective.
source: Neurons in anterior tectum, where the prey image is represented shortly before the capture strike, are tuned to larger object sizes and are frequently not direction-selective, indicating that mainly interocular comparisons serve to compute an object's movement at close range.
evidence: This is shown by the functional clustering and spatial analysis of tectal responses.

claim: Interocular comparisons serve to compute an object's movement at close range in anterior tectum.
source: Neurons in anterior tectum, where the prey image is represented shortly before the capture strike, are tuned to larger object sizes and are frequently not direction-selective, indicating that mainly interocular comparisons serve to compute an object's movement at close range.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of direction selectivity in anterior tectum and supported by the bilateral ablation experiments.

claim: The tectal feature map originates from a linear combination of diverse, functionally specialized, lamina-specific, and topographically ordered retinal ganglion cell synaptic inputs.
source: The tectal feature map originates from a linear combination of diverse, functionally specialized, lamina-specific, and topographically ordered retinal ganglion cell synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the linear modeling approach showing that tectal responses can be predicted from RGC inputs.

claim: Local cell-type composition and connectivity across the tectum are adapted to the processing of location-dependent, behaviorally relevant object features.
source: We conclude that local cell-type composition and connectivity across the tectum are adapted to the processing of location-dependent, behaviorally relevant object features.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the spatial distribution of functionally distinct cell types and their correlation with behavioral demands.

claim: The neuropil of the larval zebrafish tectum is spatially organized along the superficial-to-deep axis into layers.
source: The neuropil of the larval zebrafish tectum is spatially organized along the superficial-to-deep axis into layers, ten of which are receiving input from dedicated subsets of RGCs (Robles et al., 2013; Robles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous publications and confirmed by the anatomical analysis in this study.

claim: Ten tectal neuropil layers receive input from dedicated subsets of RGCs.
source: The neuropil of the larval zebrafish tectum is spatially organized along the superficial-to-deep axis into layers, ten of which are receiving input from dedicated subsets of RGCs (Robles et al., 2013; Robles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous work and used as a framework for the current study.

claim: Individual RGCs select one layer each, in which they arborize and make synapses onto tectal dendrites.
source: Earlier studies have shown that individual RGCs select one layer each, in which they arborize and make synapses onto tectal dendrites (Xiao and Baier, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Each retinorecipient layer contains a complete, yet feature-selective, map of visual space.
source: Thus, each retinorecipient layer contains a complete, yet feature-selective, map of visual space.
evidence: This is inferred from the layer-specific RGC projections and supported by the functional imaging data.

claim: RGCs that respond to visual features resembling the speed and size of prey project to the most superficial layer (SO).
source: RGCs that respond to visual features resembling the speed and size of prey project to the most superficial layer (SO; Semmelhack et al., 2014; see Figure 1B), whereas RGCs that are specifically tuned to a rapidly expanding (looming) dark object, simulating an approaching predator or an obstacle on a collision course, terminate in deeper layers (SFGS5/6; Temizer et al., 2015; see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is cited from previous work and confirmed by the current imaging data.

claim: RGCs tuned to rapidly expanding (looming) dark objects terminate in deeper layers (SFGS5/6).
source: RGCs that respond to visual features resembling the speed and size of prey project to the most superficial layer (SO; Semmelhack et al., 2014; see Figure 1B), whereas RGCs that are specifically tuned to a rapidly expanding (looming) dark object, simulating an approaching predator or an obstacle on a collision course, terminate in deeper layers (SFGS5/6; Temizer et al., 2015; see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is cited from previous work and confirmed by the current imaging data.

claim: Zebrafish larvae have evolved a high-acuity subarea in the temporal-ventral quadrant of the retina in which RGCs are more densely packed than in the periphery.
source: Zebrafish larvae do not possess a prima facie fovea, although they have evolved a high-acuity subarea in the temporal-ventral quadrant of the retina in which RGCs are more densely packed than in the periphery (Schmitt and Dowling, 1999; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous publications.

claim: The high-acuity retinal region holds the image of prey in the final phase of hunting behavior.
source: This region holds the image of prey in the final phase of hunting behavior and, similar to the mammalian fovea, occupies a disproportionately large area of the visual map in the tectum.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral context and anatomical organization.

claim: The high-acuity retinal region occupies a disproportionately large area of the visual map in the tectum.
source: This region holds the image of prey in the final phase of hunting behavior and, similar to the mammalian fovea, occupies a disproportionately large area of the visual map in the tectum.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of responses and anatomical considerations.

claim: Panneuronal expression of nuclear-localized calcium indicator GCaMP6s labels on average 5793 ± 202 cells per tectum in 5-7 dpf larvae.
source: At this larval stage, panneuronal expression of the nuclear-localized calcium indicator GCaMP6s (driven by the elavl3 promoter) labels on average 5793 ± 202 cells per tectum (n = 10 fish; mean ± SEM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiments.

claim: A moving dot of 5° approximates the size of prey at the onset of hunting behavior.
source: The stimulus set consisted of a moving dot of 5° ('small'), which approximates the size of prey at the onset of hunting behavior (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Patterson et al., 2013; Semmelhack et al., 2014), a moving dot of 30° ("large"), which is the approximate size of prey directly before the capture strike, and an expanding disc at different velocities, which simulates an approaching object and is able to evoke escape responses (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017; Dunn et al., 2016; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited behavioral studies.

claim: A moving dot of 30° is the approximate size of prey directly before the capture strike.
source: The stimulus set consisted of a moving dot of 5° ('small'), which approximates the size of prey at the onset of hunting behavior (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Patterson et al., 2013; Semmelhack et al., 2014), a moving dot of 30° ("large"), which is the approximate size of prey directly before the capture strike, and an expanding disc at different velocities, which simulates an approaching object and is able to evoke escape responses (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017; Dunn et al., 2016; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on behavioral measurements and cited studies.

claim: The stimulus battery obtained reproducible calcium responses in up to 30% of all tectal cells per imaging plane.
source: With this battery of visual stimuli, we obtained reproducible calcium responses in up to 30% of all tectal cells per imaging plane.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Hierarchical clustering resulted in 76 exemplars representative of 1759 sampled tectal cells in total.
source: This resulted in a dendrogram for 76 exemplars, which are representative of the 1759 sampled tectal cells in total (Figure 2B–D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct result of the clustering analysis.

claim: A minimal number of 14 clusters yielded an optimal classification of the tectal cell data.
source: A silhouette analysis to validate the clustering showed that a minimal number of 14 clusters yielded an optimal classification of the data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is determined by the silhouette analysis of the clustering.

claim: The three main principal components explain 74.9% of the variance in the tectal cell dataset.
source: Plotting the three main principal components (PCs), which could explain 74.9% of the variance in the dataset, aligned the scores along three axes for small-dot, large-dot, and looming/luminance- (OFF-) responding cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a direct result of the principal component analysis shown in the figure.

claim: 43.6% of all tectal cells responded to a looming stimulus with a score >0.2.
source: 43.6% of all cells responded to a looming stimulus (with a score >0.2), 41.1% responded to a small dot, and 33.1% responded to a large dot (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional imaging analysis.

claim: 41.1% of all tectal cells responded to a small dot.
source: 43.6% of all cells responded to a looming stimulus (with a score >0.2), 41.1% responded to a small dot, and 33.1% responded to a large dot (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional imaging analysis.

claim: 33.1% of all tectal cells responded to a large dot.
source: 43.6% of all cells responded to a looming stimulus (with a score >0.2), 41.1% responded to a small dot, and 33.1% responded to a large dot (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional imaging analysis.

claim: Only 2.7% of tectal cells responded to a bright ramp.
source: Only a small number of cells responded to a bright ramp (2.7%) or a bright flash (2.2%), and these cells were rarely sensitive to other stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional imaging analysis.

claim: Only 2.2% of tectal cells responded to a bright flash.
source: Only a small number of cells responded to a bright ramp (2.7%) or a bright flash (2.2%), and these cells were rarely sensitive to other stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional imaging analysis.

claim: The 5° grating did not trigger significant responses in the tectum.
source: The 5° grating did not trigger significant responses in the tectum, suggesting a selectivity to individual objects rather than to high spatial frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional imaging experiments.

claim: The lack of response to 5° grating suggests tectal selectivity to individual objects rather than to high spatial frequency.
source: The 5° grating did not trigger significant responses in the tectum, suggesting a selectivity to individual objects rather than to high spatial frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: The largest fraction of SINs (~45%) was mapped to the large-dot responsive cluster.
source: The largest fraction of SINs was mapped to our large-dot responsive cluster (~45%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), whereas only a small number of SINs (~6%) were sensitive to a 5° dot.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional classification of SINs.

claim: Only ~6% of SINs were sensitive to a 5° dot.
source: The largest fraction of SINs was mapped to our large-dot responsive cluster (~45%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), whereas only a small number of SINs (~6%) were sensitive to a 5° dot.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional classification of SINs.

claim: ~30% of NINs belong to the looming/dark ramp-responsive cluster.
source: Neuropil interneurons (NINs), residing within deeper layers of the neuropil, predominantly belong to the looming/dark ramp-responsive cluster (~30%), with about 20% of NINs responding to large dots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional classification of NINs.

claim: About 20% of NINs respond to large dots.
source: Neuropil interneurons (NINs), residing within deeper layers of the neuropil, predominantly belong to the looming/dark ramp-responsive cluster (~30%), with about 20% of NINs responding to large dots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional classification of NINs.

claim: The majority of tectal cells respond to object motion (small, large, or looming dots).
source: Taken together, the majority of tectal cells, both in the periventricular layer and embedded in the neuropil, respond to object motion, that is small, or large, or looming dots, sometimes in combination.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional imaging results.

claim: A substantial fraction of tectal cells responds to global dimming or looming (OFF cells).
source: A substantial fraction of cells responds to global dimming or looming (OFF cells).
evidence: This is observed in the functional imaging data.

claim: Very few tectal cells respond to global brightening (ON cells).
source: Very few cells respond to global brightening (ON cells).
evidence: This is observed in the functional imaging data.

claim: OFF and ON tectal cells are largely non-overlapping with object-detecting cells.
source: OFF and ON cells are largely non-overlapping with object-detecting cells.
evidence: This is observed in the clustering analysis of functional responses.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of RGC pixels resulted in 1157 exemplars grouped into ten functional clusters.
source: A pixel-wise regressor and cluster analysis resulted in a dendrogram for 1157 exemplars, which were grouped into ten functional clusters (although four RGC clusters resulted in the highest silhouette coefficient, we chose 10 clusters, for a significantly higher modeling correlation score, as shown below) (Figure 3A–C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct result of the clustering analysis of RGC data.

claim: 67.2% of RGC pixels responded to a large dot with a score greater than 0.2.
source: Two thirds (67.2%) of the pixels responded to a large dot with a score greater than 0.2 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RGC imaging analysis.

claim: Direction-selective responses to forward- (nasalward-) moving stimuli were more abundant than for the opposite direction in RGCs.
source: Interestingly, direction-selective responses to forward- (nasalward-) moving stimuli, especially to a large dot, were more abundant than for the opposite direction (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the RGC functional imaging data.

claim: RGC axons responding to a large dot were mainly located in the anterior-dorsal quadrant of the tectal neuropil.
source: Along the anterior-posterior (A-P) axis, we found a separation of size-selective RGC terminals. RGC axons responding to a large dot were mainly located in the anterior-dorsal quadrant of the tectal neuropil, whereas small-dot responsive pixels were found in the medial to posterior part (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the spatial distribution analysis of RGC responses.

claim: Small-dot responsive RGC pixels were found in the medial to posterior part of the tectum.
source: Along the anterior-posterior (A-P) axis, we found a separation of size-selective RGC terminals. RGC axons responding to a large dot were mainly located in the anterior-dorsal quadrant of the tectal neuropil, whereas small-dot responsive pixels were found in the medial to posterior part (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the spatial distribution analysis of RGC responses.

claim: Most tectal cell responses could be well explained by a linear combination of on average two RGC input clusters.
source: Most tectal cell responses could be well explained by a linear combination of on average two RGC input clusters (Figure 4D);~36% of all responses could even be predicted by a single RGC input weight.
evidence: This is a result of the linear modeling analysis.

claim: ~36% of all tectal responses could be predicted by a single RGC input weight.
source: Most tectal cell responses could be well explained by a linear combination of on average two RGC input clusters (Figure 4D);~36% of all responses could even be predicted by a single RGC input weight.
evidence: This is a result of the linear modeling analysis.

claim: The linear modeling approach resulted in a high prediction quality with median correlation R2score = 0.68.
source: Modeling the scores for each of the 1759 tectal cells resulted in a high prediction quality (median correlation R2score = 0.68, median RMSE = 0.06; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result of the modeling analysis.

claim: Most visual representations in the tectum are directly inherited from RGC inputs.
source: Our modeling results suggest that most visual representations in the tectum are directly inherited from RGC inputs.
evidence: This is concluded from the high prediction quality of the linear model.

claim: Non-retinal, presumably intratectal computations add feature specificities such as information on the direction of small moving objects.
source: In addition, non-retinal, presumably intratectal computations add feature specificities, such as information on the direction of small moving objects, and sharpen both object-size and luminance selectivities of tectal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancies between the model predictions and measured responses, particularly for direction selectivity.

claim: Intratectal computations sharpen object-size and luminance selectivities of tectal neurons.
source: In addition, non-retinal, presumably intratectal computations add feature specificities, such as information on the direction of small moving objects, and sharpen both object-size and luminance selectivities of tectal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing that tectal responses are more selective than predicted from RGC inputs alone.

claim: RGC axons sensitive to small dots enter the tectum in superficial layers (SO to SFGS4) with a peak in SFGS1/2.
source: Along the superficial-to-deep axis, in line with previous publications, we found that RGC axons sensitive to small dots enter the tectum in superficial layers (SO to SFGS4) with a peak in SFGS1/2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Preuss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown by the layer-specific quantification of RGC responses and is consistent with cited previous work.

claim: Direction-selective RGC pixels were located most superficially in the posterior half of SFGS1.
source: DS pixels were located most superficially in the posterior half of SFGS1 (Figure 3C; Nikolaou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown by the spatial distribution analysis and is consistent with cited previous work.

claim: OFF-responsive RGC axons arborized in deep SFGS layers, SGC and SAC/SPV, and most extensively in SFGS5/6.
source: OFF-responsive axons, on the other hand, arborized in deep SFGS layers, SGC and SAC/SPV, and most extensively in SFGS5/6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown by the layer-specific quantification of RGC responses and is consistent with cited previous work.

claim: Small- and large-dot responsive tectal cells showed significantly denser arborizations in SO, SFGS1/2, and SFGS3/4 compared to OFF cells.
source: In addition, we found that small- and large-dot responsive cells showed significantly denser arborizations in SO, SFGS1/2, and SFGS3/4 compared to OFF cells.
evidence: This is a result of the morphological quantification of FuGIMA-labeled cells.

claim: OFF cells were biased to extend neurites in the SGC, the SAC, SAC/SPV and the SM.
source: OFF cells, on the other hand, were biased to extend neurites in the SGC, the SAC, SAC/SPV and the SM (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result of the morphological quantification of FuGIMA-labeled cells.

claim: SM is a layer at the surface of the tectum, which is innervated by the torus longitudinalis, a higher-order visual area with strong OFF responses.
source: SM is a layer at the surface of the tectum, which is innervated by the torus longitudinalis, a higher-order visual area with strong OFF responses (Northmore, 1984; Robles et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Single cell arbors were generally small in superficial layers (SM to SFGS3-4) and largest in deeper layers (SFGS5-6 to SAC/SPV).
source: We found that single cell arbors were generally small in superficial layers (SM to SFGS3-4) and largest in deeper layers (SFGS5-6 to SAC/SPV; Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a result of the morphological quantification of arbor areas.

claim: Small-dot responsive cells have a columnar shape on average.
source: While on average, small-dot responsive cells have a columnar shape, OFF cells have extended arbors in deeper layers, rendering them cone-shaped (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This is a result of the morphological analysis comparing arbor ratios.

claim: OFF cells have extended arbors in deeper layers, rendering them cone-shaped.
source: While on average, small-dot responsive cells have a columnar shape, OFF cells have extended arbors in deeper layers, rendering them cone-shaped (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This is a result of the morphological analysis comparing arbor ratios.

claim: Object-motion responsive and OFF cells target layers that match their corresponding retinal inputs.
source: Object-motion responsive and OFF cells thus target layers that match their corresponding retinal and, in the case of SM, non-retinal inputs and also differ in more subtle morphological features.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation between functional responses and dendritic arborization patterns.

claim: The large-dot response cluster was shifted to the anterior tectum compared to all sampled cells.
source: Compared to all sampled cells, the large-dot response cluster was shifted to the anterior tectum, while cell bodies responding to small dots were biased to the posterior region.
evidence: This is shown by the spatial distribution analysis of cell body positions.

claim: Cell bodies responding to small dots were biased to the posterior region of the tectum.
source: Compared to all sampled cells, the large-dot response cluster was shifted to the anterior tectum, while cell bodies responding to small dots were biased to the posterior region.
evidence: This is shown by the spatial distribution analysis of cell body positions.

claim: The strongest posterior bias was found for direction-selective cell bodies, responsive to a small, forward moving dot.
source: The strongest posterior bias was found for direction-selective cell bodies, responsive to a small, forward moving dot (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by the spatial distribution analysis of cell body positions.

claim: ~90% of neurites from DS small-dot responsive cells were found in the posterior half of the tectum.
source: We found the same effect, that is large-dot responsive cells arborize more extensively in the anterior neuropil, compared to all sampled interneurons, while ~90% of neurites from DS small-dot responsive cells were found in the posterior half (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is a result of the quantification of neurite distribution in FuGIMA cells.

claim: Laser ablation of the RGC axon bundle that leaves AF7 achieved selective disruption of small-object input to the SO layer.
source: By laser ablation of the RGC axon bundle that leaves AF7, we achieved selective disruption of small-object input to the SO layer (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ablation experiment and subsequent functional imaging.

claim: Small-dot responses were significantly diminished in tectal cells after ablation of RGC axons projecting to SO.
source: Functional calcium imaging before and after the ablations revealed that small-dot responses were significantly diminished in tectal cells (Figure 7D, E and G).
evidence: This is a direct result of the ablation experiment.

claim: The number of looming-responsive cells in the affected tectum was not reduced after RGC ablation, but even increased in some animals.
source: In contrast, the number of looming-responsive cells in the affected tectum was not reduced, but even increased in some animals, possibly due to the loss of inhibition by the small-object-processing circuit (see Barker and Baier, 2015; Figure 7D, F and G).
evidence: This is a result of the ablation experiment.

claim: The increase in looming-responsive cells after small-object RGC ablation is possibly due to the loss of inhibition by the small-object-processing circuit.
source: In contrast, the number of looming-responsive cells in the affected tectum was not reduced, but even increased in some animals, possibly due to the loss of inhibition by the small-object-processing circuit (see Barker and Baier, 2015; Figure 7D, F and G).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental result, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RGC projections to SO are essential for tectal cells to assume their tuning to small-object motion.
source: These results indicate that RGC projections to SO are essential for tectal cells to assume their tuning to small-object motion.
evidence: This is concluded from the ablation experiment results.

claim: A prey object of 250 µm length at 3 mm distance subtends a visual angle of approximately 5°.
source: A typical prey object, such as a paramecium or a rotifer, of 250 µm length, which is 3 mm away, subtends a visual angle of approximately 5°.
evidence: This is a geometric calculation based on the size and distance of prey.

claim: The fish executes a capture strike when the prey is in the upper central field of both eyes at a distance range of 0.3–0.7 mm.
source: The fish executes a capture strike when the prey is in the upper central field of both eyes at a distance range of 0.3–0.7 mm (Mearns et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a previous behavioral study.

claim: Prey at 0.3–0.7 mm distance corresponds to 20–40° of visual angle.
source: This corresponds to 20–40° of visual angle.
evidence: This is a geometric calculation based on prey size and distance.

claim: Following removal of large-dot responsive cells, animals spent less time with their eyes converged.
source: Following removal of large-dot responsive cells, animals spent less time with their eyes converged, indicating less time spent engaged in hunting behavior (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a direct result of the ablation and behavioral analysis experiment.

claim: After ablation of large-dot responsive cells in the right tectum, J-turns were biased to the right side.
source: In addition, their J-turns were biased to the right side, indicating defective prey detection by the left eye or right (ablated) tectum, respectively (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is a direct result of the ablation and behavioral analysis experiment.

claim: Control fish in which entirely non-responsive cells were ablated showed no effect on prey capture behavior.
source: Control fish, in which entirely non-responsive cells were ablated, showed no effect on prey capture behavior and were indistinguishable from untreated or agarose-embedded larvae (Figure 8A–D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a result of the control ablation experiments.

claim: Ablation of small-dot responsive cells did not result in significant behavioral changes.
source: Likewise, ablation of small-dot responsive cells, either in the anterior or posterior tectum did not result in significant behavioral changes (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This is a result of the ablation and behavioral analysis experiment.

claim: For cells which tile the visual field by only 5°, the ablated cell numbers were not sufficient to observe an effect on behavior.
source: This suggests that for cells, which tile the visual field by only 5°, the ablated cell numbers were not sufficient to observe an effect on behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why small-dot cell ablations did not affect behavior.

claim: A substantial number of cells in the left tectum were responsive to prey-like stimuli presented to the left (ipsilateral) eye.
source: Intriguingly, we observed in our imaging experiments, that a substantial number of cells in the left tectum were responsive to prey-like stimuli presented to the left (ipsilateral) eye (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Ipsilaterally responsive tectal cells are probably activated by the contralateral tectum via an intertectal commissure.
source: These cells are probably activated by the right (contralateral) tectum via an intertectal commissure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of ipsilateral responses and anatomical knowledge.

claim: In bilaterally ablated animals, the tendency to increase right J-turns and reduce left J-turns in response to prey was more pronounced than in right-tectum-only ablated larvae.
source: In bilaterally ablated animals, the tendency to increase right J-turns and reduce left J-turns in response to prey was even more pronounced than in right-tectum-only ablated larvae, supporting our hypothesis.
evidence: This is a result of the bilateral ablation experiment.

claim: In fish with the right eye removed, there was a significant increase in the number of large-dot responsive cells in the right, visually stimulated tectum.
source: In these animals, we observed a significant increase in the number of large-dot responsive cells in the right, visually stimulated tectum, that is ipsilateral to the enucleated side.
evidence: This is a result of the enucleation experiment.

claim: Stimulus-evoked activity is normally dampened by background activity in the contralateral tectum by intertectal inhibitory connections.
source: This result suggests that stimulus-evoked activity is normally dampened by background activity in the contralateral tectum by intertectal inhibitory connections.
evidence: This is inferred from the enucleation experiment results.

claim: The tectum is critically involved in identification, localization, pursuit, and capture of prey.
source: The tectum is critically involved in identification, localization, pursuit, and capture of prey (Gahtan et al., 2005; Semmelhack et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Small, sideways-moving dots are readily approached by zebrafish larvae.
source: In previous studies, we discovered that this distinction is made by size and movement characteristics of the perceived object (Barker and Baier, 2015). Small, sideways-moving dots are readily approached (Semmelhack et al., 2014), whereas expanding (looming) dots, displayed to the side of the fish while it is immobilized, are categorized as threatening and avoided by vigorous escape attempts (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous behavioral studies.

claim: Expanding (looming) dots are categorized as threatening and avoided by vigorous escape attempts.
source: Small, sideways-moving dots are readily approached (Semmelhack et al., 2014), whereas expanding (looming) dots, displayed to the side of the fish while it is immobilized, are categorized as threatening and avoided by vigorous escape attempts (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous behavioral studies.

claim: Retinal inputs carrying prey-like signals mainly enter the tectum in layers SO and SFGS1-4.
source: Retinal inputs carrying prey-like signals mainly enter the tectum in layers SO and SFGS1-4, and looming-sensitive RGC axons are largely restricted to SFGS5/6 and SGC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RGC imaging and layer quantification.

claim: Looming-sensitive RGC axons are largely restricted to SFGS5/6 and SGC.
source: Retinal inputs carrying prey-like signals mainly enter the tectum in layers SO and SFGS1-4, and looming-sensitive RGC axons are largely restricted to SFGS5/6 and SGC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RGC imaging and layer quantification.

claim: Broadly-tuned OFF signals are transmitted to the deep retinorecipient layers SGC and SAC/SPV.
source: In addition, broadly-tuned OFF signals are transmitted to the deep retinorecipient layers SGC and SAC/SPV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RGC imaging and layer quantification.

claim: Prey-selective tectal neurons extend dendrite branches into the superficial layers of the tectum.
source: Prey-selective neurons extend dendrite branches into the superficial layers of the tectum, while looming-sensitive neurons tend to arborize in middle to deep layers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FuGIMA morphological analysis.

claim: Looming-sensitive tectal neurons tend to arborize in middle to deep layers.
source: Prey-selective neurons extend dendrite branches into the superficial layers of the tectum, while looming-sensitive neurons tend to arborize in middle to deep layers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FuGIMA morphological analysis.

claim: More than a third of the tectal response classes match a single RGC input class.
source: A simple excitation-only, feed-forward model showed that more than a third of the tectal response classes match a single RGC input class.
evidence: This is a result of the linear modeling analysis.

claim: The vast majority of the remaining tectal responses were explained by a linear combination of two, or sometimes more, RGC inputs.
source: The vast majority of the remaining responses were explained by a linear combination of two, or sometimes more, RGC inputs.
evidence: This is a result of the linear modeling analysis.

claim: The zebrafish tectum is not merely a passive relay station for retinal inputs.
source: The zebrafish tectum, however, is not merely a passive relay station for retinal inputs.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results showing that some tectal features cannot be explained by RGC inputs alone.

claim: Responses to large objects are markedly reduced in the tectum compared to RGCs.
source: First, we found that responses to large objects are markedly reduced in the tectum compared to RGCs.
evidence: This is observed by comparing RGC and tectal response distributions.

claim: Direction selectivity to backward-moving objects is calculated de novo in the tectum.
source: Second, direction selectivity to backward-moving objects is calculated de novo in the tectum.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results showing poor prediction of direction selectivity from RGC inputs.

claim: A circuit involving feed-forward inhibition by SINs could account for the de novo computation of direction selectivity.
source: A circuit involving feed-forward inhibition by SINs, which suppresses tectal responses to non-preferred directions, could account for this computation (Abbas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on cited previous work.

claim: A substantial number of tectal cells selectively respond to a dark ramp stimulus, which were not observed in the RGC dataset.
source: Third, a substantial number of tectal cells selectively respond to a dark ramp stimulus; such cells were not observed in our RGC dataset.
evidence: This is observed by comparing tectal and RGC response profiles.

claim: Tectum-intrinsic circuitry adds direction selectivity to a subset of channels and generally refines and sharpens the responses.
source: Thus, tectum-intrinsic circuitry adds direction selectivity to a subset of channels and generally refines and sharpens the responses.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of RGC and tectal responses and the modeling results.

claim: The anatomical separation of small-dot responsive and looming-sensitive circuits probably reflects functional segregation of the two processing streams.
source: The anatomical separation of small-dot responsive and looming-sensitive circuits probably reflects functional segregation of the two processing streams.
evidence: This is inferred from the laminar organization of RGC inputs and tectal cell dendrites.

claim: Barker and Baier, 2015 postulated a circuit motif that implements balanced, reciprocal inhibition of approach vs. avoidance systems.
source: Barker and Baier, 2015 postulated a circuit motif that implements balanced, reciprocal inhibition of the two systems driving approach vs. avoidance.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Bundling in space the visual processing of object valence, global patterns and luminance levels by laminar separation may serve to minimize wiring lengths.
source: Moreover, bundling in space the visual processing of object valence, global patterns and luminance levels by laminar separation may also serve to minimize wiring lengths of the corresponding neural elements in the tectal neuropil (Baier, 2013; Chklovskii et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a proposed functional explanation supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Larval zebrafish are able to detect a prey item at a distance of several millimeters.
source: Larval zebrafish are able to detect a prey item at a distance of several millimeters.
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations.

claim: Moving dots of 1° rarely elicited a response in head-fixed larvae.
source: Moving dots of 1° rarely elicited a response.
evidence: This is an observation from functional imaging experiments.

claim: 1° is the resolution limit of the larval fish's visual system.
source: This seems to be the resolution limit of the larval fish's visual system and is in agreement with the physical limit posed by photoreceptor spacing in the retina (Haug et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral responses and supported by cited anatomical data.

claim: More than half of all large dot-responsive cells also responded to a slow-looming stimulus.
source: Interestingly, this overlap is negligible for fast looming stimuli, what might indicate a separation of approach and avoidance circuits.
evidence: This is observed in the functional clustering analysis.

claim: The overlap between large-dot and fast-looming responses is negligible, which might indicate a separation of approach and avoidance circuits.
source: Interestingly, this overlap is negligible for fast looming stimuli, what might indicate a separation of approach and avoidance circuits.
evidence: This is observed in the functional clustering analysis and interpreted as evidence for circuit segregation.

claim: An overrepresentation of small-dot responsive, direction-selective cells in the posterior tectum appears to be an adaptation to the preponderance of small prey objects in the peripheral field of view.
source: First, an overrepresentation of small-dot responsive, direction-selective cells in the posterior tectum appears to be an adaptation to the preponderance of small prey objects in the peripheral field of view, whose movement is, at least initially, independent of the fish's own.
evidence: This is concluded from the spatial distribution of functionally distinct cells and their behavioral relevance.

claim: Posterior tectal cells acquire their direction selectivity by de novo computations from size-tuned, non-DS RGC inputs.
source: These tectal cells acquire their direction selectivity by de novo computations from size-tuned, non-DS RGC inputs (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results and ablation experiments.

claim: Determining the direction of prey by a local mechanism is particularly important for the lateral field of view, which is entirely monocular.
source: Determining the direction of prey by a local mechanism is particularly important for the lateral field of view, which is entirely monocular.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomy and behavioral demands.

claim: Fish will preferentially orient towards prey in their lateral visual field, because it gives them more time to move their body into the right position for a successful strike.
source: Fish will preferentially orient towards prey in their lateral visual field, because it gives them more time to move their body into the right position for a successful strike.
evidence: This is a behavioral interpretation based on the spatial organization of the visual system.

claim: Turning is energetically costly and may alert nearby predators and prey alike.
source: Moreover, turning is energetically costly and may alert nearby predators and prey alike.
evidence: This is general knowledge about animal behavior.

claim: Zebrafish larvae have been observed to use a sit-and-wait mode of hunting.
source: Zebrafish larvae have been observed to use such a sit-and-wait mode of hunting (Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from a previous behavioral study.

claim: Large-dot responsive tectal cells facilitate the initiation of prey capture-associated J-turns.
source: Second, the anterior tectum is enriched for large-dot responsive tectal cells (Figure 8E), which appear to facilitate the initiation of prey capture-associated J-turns, as shown here by laser ablation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ablation and behavioral experiments.

claim: J-turns are fine adjustments of body posture characteristic of hunting.
source: J-turns are fine adjustments of body posture characteristic of hunting.
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations.

claim: Large-dot selective cells communicate via commissural connections with the contralateral tectum.
source: These cells are frequently not direction-selective and communicate via commissural connections with the contralateral tectum.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging experiments showing ipsilateral responses.

claim: Activation of large-dot selective cells suppresses responses in the contralateral tectum.
source: Initial imaging and behavioral experiments following ablations suggest that activation of large-dot selective cells suppresses responses in the contralateral tectum.
evidence: This is inferred from the bilateral ablation and enucleation experiments.

claim: An intertectal inhibitory mechanism helps to correct slight displacements of the prey from the midline.
source: We propose that such an intertectal inhibitory mechanism helps to correct slight displacements of the prey from the midline (see also Gebhardt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental results and cited work.

claim: The visual map in the tectum is not a veridical, unbiased representation of all positions in visible space, but rather warped by location-dependent feature statistics.
source: The visual map in the tectum is thus not a veridical, unbiased representation of all positions in visible space, but rather warped by location-dependent feature statistics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.
